content: A crisis hotline is a dedicated telephone service that individuals can contact to receive immediate, over-the-phone emergency counseling. These hotlines are typically staffed by trained volunteers who provide support to individuals in distress. The concept of crisis hotlines has been present in most major cities across the United States since at least the mid-1970s. Initially, these services were established to assist individuals contemplating suicide. Over time, their scope has broadened to address a wide range of emotional crises. In addition to suicide prevention, crisis hotlines now cater to individuals facing various challenges, such as survivors of sexual assault, runaway children, and members of the LGBTQ+ community. The origins of such services date back to 1953, when Chad Varah, an English vicar, founded The Samaritans, a service that quickly expanded across the United Kingdom. In the United States, the San Francisco Suicide Prevention organization launched a hotline called Call Bruce in 1962. Similarly, Australia established its own crisis hotline, Lifeline, in 1963. In 1968, a fully volunteer-operated crisis hotline known as Lifelink Samaritans was founded in Tasmania by concerned citizens of Launceston. This service provides 24/7 emotional support to callers throughout Tasmania and operates without any religious affiliations. Lifelink Samaritans is a member of Befrienders Worldwide and maintains a twinning partnership with Northampton Samaritans in the United Kingdom. It holds the distinction of being the oldest telephone befriending service in Tasmania and the fourth oldest in Australia. Historically, suicide hotlines faced criticism for their perceived limitations. One concern was that individuals who were resolute in their decision to end their lives might not reach out for help. Additionally, those suffering from social anxiety might lack the emotional capacity to make such a call. For many years, there was no concrete evidence to suggest that the existence of suicide hotlines had a measurable impact on reducing suicide rates. However, a pivotal study conducted in 2007 disproved this notion. The study demonstrated that individuals who contacted crisis hotlines experienced a reduction in suicidal thoughts during the call itself, and this effect persisted for several weeks following the interaction.
